Bonding.intro: Atoms bond together to form compounds. There are three main types of chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic.
Bonding.mnemonic: Use 'ICM' for the three bond types: Ionic = metal + non-metal (electrons Transferred); Covalent = non-metal + non-metal (electrons Shared); Metallic = metal + metal (electrons Delocalised). Or: 'I Transfer, C Shares, M Delocalises'.

sections.title: Types of Bond
sections.text: The type of bond formed depends on the elements involved. Ionic bonding involves electron transfer; covalent involves sharing; metallic involves a sea of delocalised electrons.
points: Ionic bonding — transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal; forms oppositely charged ions that attract
Covalent bonding — sharing of a pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms; both atoms count the shared electrons
Metallic bonding — positive metal ions in a lattice surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons
Rule of thumb — metal + non-metal → ionic; non-metal + non-metal → covalent; metal + metal → metallic
Electronegativity — atoms bond to achieve a full outer shell (octet rule — usually 8 electrons)

sections.title: Electron Shells and Bonding
sections.text: Atoms bond because doing so gives them a full outer electron shell, which is a more stable arrangement.
points: Octet rule — most atoms aim for 8 outer electrons (like the nearest noble gas)
Hydrogen exception — needs only 2 outer electrons (like helium)
Dot-and-cross diagrams — show outer electrons only; X from one atom, dot from the other
Ionic dot-and-cross — show electron transfer with square brackets and charge on each ion
Covalent dot-and-cross — show shared pairs between atoms; each atom in the bond has a full outer shell

callout.label: Why Bond?
callout.text: Atoms bond to achieve a full outer electron shell (usually 8 — octet rule). Bonding makes atoms more stable.

sections.title: Bonding and Properties Overview
sections.text: The type of bonding determines the structure and properties of a substance — including melting point, conductivity, and hardness.
points: Ionic compounds — giant lattice; high melting point; conduct when molten/dissolved; brittle
Simple molecular covalent — small molecules; low melting point; do not conduct electricity
Giant covalent — millions of covalent bonds; very high melting point; generally do not conduct (except graphite)
Metallic — giant metallic lattice; high melting point; conduct electricity and heat; malleable
Predicting structure from bonding — ionic or metallic = giant structure; simple molecular = low MP; giant covalent = very high MP, no conduction

keyTerms.def: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer
A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms
Electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons
The tendency of atoms to form bonds to achieve 8 outer electrons (full outer shell)
A diagram showing the outer electrons of atoms in a bond, using dots and crosses to distinguish atoms
Electrons not associated with a specific atom; free to move — present in metals and graphite

examTips: Ionic = metal + non-metal (electrons TRANSFERRED). Covalent = non-metal + non-metal (electrons SHARED). Metallic = metal only (electrons DELOCALISED).
Always draw dot-and-cross diagrams showing full outer shells — only draw outer shell electrons, not all electrons.
When asked to explain bonding, name the type of bond AND describe the interaction (e.g. 'electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions').
commonMistakes: Saying electrons are shared in ionic bonding — they are TRANSFERRED from the metal to the non-metal.
Drawing inner shells on dot-and-cross diagrams — only draw outer shell electrons.
Forgetting that covalent bonding can only occur between non-metals — metal + non-metal is always ionic.
clozePassages: There are three main types of chemical bonding. Ionic bonding involves the transfer of electrons from metals to non-metals, forming oppositely charged ions that attract each other. Covalent bonding involves the sharing of electrons between non-metal atoms. Metallic bonding involves a lattice of positive ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. The type of bonding determines the properties of the substance.

The type of bonding in a substance determines its properties. Ionic compounds have high melting points, are brittle, and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved. Covalent substances generally have lower melting points. Metals are good conductors of electricity and heat due to delocalised electrons. Understanding bonding helps predict whether a substance will be solid, liquid, or gas at room temperature and how it will react.

Atoms form bonds to achieve a stable electronic configuration — usually a full outer shell. In ionic bonding, metals lose electrons to form positive cations and non-metals gain electrons to form negative anions. The opposite charges attract, forming an ionic lattice. In covalent bonding, atoms share pairs of electrons. Each shared pair forms one covalent bond. Some atoms can form double or triple bonds by sharing more than one pair of electrons.

Ionic Compounds.intro: Ionic compounds form when electrons are transferred from metals to non-metals, creating oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic forces.
Ionic Compounds.mnemonic: Remember 'Metal Loses, Non-metal Gains' — MLNG. Metals are Losing electrons (go positive); Non-metals are Gaining electrons (go negative). And: 'Cats Are Positive, An-ions Are Negative' (cation = positive, anion = negative).

sections.title: Forming Ions
sections.text: Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons. Metals lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions.
points: Metal loses electrons → forms positive ion (cation), e.g. Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
Non-metal gains electrons → forms negative ion (anion), e.g. Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻
Ions have full outer shells — same electronic configuration as the nearest noble gas
Common ions — Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, Cl⁻, O²⁻, S²⁻
Group links — Group 1 forms 1+ ions; Group 2 forms 2+ ions; Group 6 forms 2− ions; Group 7 forms 1− ions
Giant ionic lattice — each ion surrounded by oppositely charged ions in a regular 3D arrangement

sections.title: Properties of Ionic Compounds
sections.text: The giant ionic lattice structure explains the key properties of ionic compounds: high melting points, brittleness, and electrical conductivity only when ions are free to move.
points: High melting/boiling points — strong electrostatic forces throughout the lattice require a lot of energy to overcome
Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved — ions are free to move and carry charge
Do NOT conduct electricity as solids — ions held in fixed positions in the lattice, cannot move
Brittle — when struck, layers of ions shift so like charges align and repel, shattering the structure
Often soluble in water — water molecules can surround and separate the ions
Higher charge = stronger forces — e.g. MgO (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻) has higher MP than NaCl (Na⁺ and Cl⁻)

sections.title: Writing Ionic Formulas
sections.text: Ionic formulas are written so that the overall charge is zero — the charges on cations and anions must balance.
points: Balancing charges — total positive charge must equal total negative charge
Example: NaCl — Na⁺ and Cl⁻; charges balance (1+ and 1−); formula = NaCl
Example: MgCl₂ — Mg²⁺ and 2 × Cl⁻; 2+ balanced by 2×1−; formula = MgCl₂
Example: Al₂O₃ — 2 × Al³⁺ and 3 × O²⁻; total charge = 6+ and 6−; balanced
Polyatomic ions — e.g. OH⁻, SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻; treat as single units when balancing

keyTerms.def: An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons and has an overall charge
A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons (metals)
A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains electrons (non-metals)
A regular 3D arrangement of ions in an ionic compound, held together by electrostatic forces
The force of attraction between oppositely charged ions — the basis of ionic bonding
A substance that has been melted to a liquid — ionic compounds can conduct electricity when molten

examTips: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when MOLTEN or in SOLUTION — not when solid; ions must be free to move.
Higher charge on ions means stronger electrostatic forces and higher melting point — compare MgO (very high MP) with NaCl.
When drawing dot-and-cross for ionic compounds, use square brackets with the charge outside for each ion.
commonMistakes: Saying ionic compounds conduct electricity as solids — they cannot; ions are in fixed positions in the lattice.
Forgetting that ALL ionic compounds have high melting points due to the strong forces throughout the giant lattice.
Writing wrong ionic charges — remember Group 1 → 1+, Group 2 → 2+, Group 6 → 2−, Group 7 → 1−.
clozePassages: Ionic compounds consist of a regular lattice of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction. They have high melting points because a large amount of energy is needed to break the lattice. They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water because the ions are free to move, but not when solid. Ionic compounds are typically brittle and crystalline.

Common ionic compounds include sodium chloride (NaCl), formed when sodium gives an electron to chlorine. Sodium forms a Na⁺ ion and chlorine forms a Cl⁻ ion. These oppositely charged ions are attracted and form a giant ionic lattice. The properties of ionic compounds — including their high melting points and solubility — result from the strength of the electrostatic forces holding the lattice together.

Electrolysis can decompose ionic compounds. When an ionic compound is molten or dissolved, the ions are free to move to the electrodes. Positive ions (cations) move to the negative electrode (cathode) where they gain electrons and are reduced. Negative ions (anions) move to the positive electrode (anode) where they lose electrons and are oxidised. This principle is used to extract reactive metals like aluminium.

Covalent Substances.intro: Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share electrons. Covalent substances can have simple molecular or giant covalent structures.
Covalent Substances.mnemonic: For simple vs giant covalent: 'Simple is Small and Soft (low MP); Giant is Grand and Hard (high MP).' For diamond vs graphite: 'Diamond is 4-bonded Dense and Doesn't conduct; Graphite is 3-bonded, layers Glide, conducts electricity.'

sections.title: Simple Molecular Substances
sections.text: Simple molecular substances have strong covalent bonds within molecules but only weak intermolecular forces between molecules. This gives them low melting points.
points: Strong covalent bonds within molecules — lots of energy needed to break these
Weak intermolecular forces between molecules — little energy needed to separate them
Low melting and boiling points — only the weak intermolecular forces are broken on melting/boiling
Do NOT conduct electricity — no ions or free electrons present
Examples — H₂O, CO₂, O₂, NH₃, CH₄, HCl, Cl₂
Larger molecules = stronger intermolecular forces — e.g. iodine (I₂) is a solid at room temperature

sections.title: Giant Covalent Structures
sections.text: Giant covalent structures have millions of atoms bonded covalently in a 3D network. Breaking down the structure requires breaking many strong covalent bonds, so melting points are extremely high.
points: Giant 3D lattice — millions of covalent bonds throughout the structure
Very high melting/boiling points — must break many strong covalent bonds to melt
Generally do not conduct electricity — no free electrons or ions (exception: graphite and graphene)
Diamond — hardest natural substance; each C bonded to 4 others tetrahedrally; no free electrons
Silicon dioxide (SiO₂) — sand/quartz; each Si bonded to 4 O atoms; very hard; high MP
Graphite and graphene — each C bonded to 3 others; delocalised electrons allow conduction

sections.title: Diamond vs Graphite
sections.text: Diamond and graphite are both forms of pure carbon but have very different structures and properties — they are allotropes of carbon.
points: Diamond — each C bonded to 4 others; tetrahedral 3D structure; very hard; no free electrons; does not conduct
Graphite — each C bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers; 1 delocalised electron per C atom
Graphite conducts — delocalised electrons move through the layers; used as electrodes
Graphite is a lubricant — layers held by weak forces; can slide over each other easily
Graphene — single layer of graphite; one atom thick; incredibly strong and lightweight; good conductor
Fullerenes (e.g. C₆₀) — hollow carbon cages or tubes; used in nanotechnology and drug delivery

keyTerms.def: Substance made of small covalently bonded molecules with weak intermolecular forces between them
Substance with millions of atoms all covalently bonded in a 3D lattice; very high melting points
An electron not associated with a specific atom — allows graphite to conduct electricity
A force between molecules — weaker than the covalent bonds within molecules; overcome on melting
Different structural forms of the same element — diamond, graphite, and graphene are allotropes of carbon
A single layer of graphite — one atom thick, extremely strong, and conducts electricity
A hollow cage or tube of carbon atoms, e.g. buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) or carbon nanotubes

examTips: Simple molecular = low melting point. Giant covalent = very high melting point — the key distinction in exam questions.
Graphite conducts electricity because it has delocalised electrons — diamond does NOT conduct; it has no free electrons.
When explaining low melting points of simple molecular substances, always say 'only the weak intermolecular forces are broken — the covalent bonds within molecules remain intact'.
commonMistakes: Saying all covalent substances have low melting points — GIANT covalent structures (diamond, SiO₂) have very HIGH melting points.
Forgetting graphite is the exception — it DOES conduct electricity due to delocalised electrons between layers.
Saying 'covalent bonds are broken on melting' for simple molecular substances — only intermolecular forces are broken, NOT the covalent bonds.
clozePassages: Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons. Simple molecular substances such as water (H₂O) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) have strong covalent bonds within molecules but weak intermolecular forces between them. This gives them low melting and boiling points. They do not conduct electricity because they have no free electrons or ions.

Giant covalent structures have atoms held together by strong covalent bonds throughout the structure. Diamond has each carbon atom bonded to four others in a tetrahedral lattice, making it extremely hard with a very high melting point. Graphite has layers of carbon atoms where each carbon is bonded to three others. The layers can slide over each other, making it soft and slippery. Delocalised electrons between layers make graphite a good conductor of electricity.

Fullerenes are molecular forms of carbon. Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) consists of 60 carbon atoms arranged in a spherical cage of hexagons and pentagons. Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with remarkable strength and electrical conductivity. These properties make them useful in nanotechnology, drug delivery, and as reinforcing materials. Graphene is a single layer of graphite and is the thinnest, strongest material known.

Metallic Structures.intro: Metals have a unique bonding structure that explains their characteristic properties.
Metallic Structures.mnemonic: Think 'Positive Ions in a Sea of Electrons' — PISE. The sea of delocalised electrons explains ALL metal properties: Conduction (electrons flow), Malleability (ions slide, electrons move with them), High melting point (strong attraction throughout).

sections.title: Metallic Bonding
sections.text: In metallic bonding, metal atoms release their outer electrons to form a 'sea' of delocalised electrons surrounding a lattice of positive metal ions.
points: Positive metal ions in a regular giant lattice structure
Sea of delocalised electrons — outer electrons released and free to move throughout the structure
Strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the negative electron sea holds the structure together
Giant metallic lattice — extends throughout the entire piece of metal
More outer electrons = stronger bonding — e.g. Mg (2 outer electrons) has higher MP than Na (1 outer electron)

sections.title: Properties of Metals
sections.text: All metallic properties can be explained by the giant metallic lattice structure with delocalised electrons.
points: High melting/boiling points — strong metallic bonds throughout the giant lattice require a lot of energy to break
Conduct electricity — delocalised electrons carry charge through the structure; works as a solid AND liquid
Conduct heat — delocalised electrons transfer kinetic energy rapidly through the metal
Malleable and ductile — layers of positive ions can slide over each other; electrons move too, maintaining bonds
Shiny when polished — delocalised electrons reflect light from the surface
Alloys are harder — different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, preventing sliding → stronger than pure metals

sections.title: Alloys
sections.text: Alloys are mixtures of metals (or metals with other elements) that have improved properties compared to pure metals.
points: Definition — mixture of a metal with one or more other elements
Why harder — different-sized atoms disrupt the regular lattice, preventing layers from sliding over each other
Steel — iron + carbon (and other metals); harder, stronger, and more resistant to corrosion than pure iron
Bronze — copper + tin; harder than either pure metal; used for tools, statues, bearings
Brass — copper + zinc; used in musical instruments, plumbing fittings
Nitinol — nickel + titanium; shape memory alloy — returns to original shape when heated

keyTerms.def: Electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons
A mixture of a metal with another element to improve properties such as hardness or corrosion resistance
The ability of a metal to be hammered into a new shape without breaking — due to sliding ion layers
Able to be drawn into wires — a property of metals due to their structure
Electrons free to move throughout a metallic lattice — responsible for conduction of electricity and heat
The regular 3D arrangement of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons

examTips: Always link metallic properties back to delocalised electrons — say 'delocalised electrons' not just 'free electrons'.
Alloys are harder than pure metals because different-sized atoms distort the regular lattice, preventing layers from sliding — state this mechanism explicitly.
For malleability: layers of ions CAN slide because electrons move with them — the bond is not broken.
commonMistakes: Writing 'free electrons' instead of 'delocalised electrons' — AQA mark schemes expect the term 'delocalised'.
Forgetting WHY alloys are harder — not just 'different atoms', but 'different-sized atoms disrupt the regular lattice, preventing sliding'.
Saying metals only conduct electricity — they also conduct heat well, via the same delocalised electrons.
clozePassages: In metallic bonding, metal atoms release their outer electrons to form a lattice of positive ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. The strong attraction between the positive ions and the electron sea holds the structure together. This explains many properties of metals — they are good conductors of electricity and heat because the delocalised electrons can move freely throughout the structure.

Metals are malleable (can be hammered into shape) and ductile (can be drawn into wires) because the layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bonds. Alloys are mixtures of metals or metals with other elements. The atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular lattice, preventing layers from sliding, making alloys harder and stronger than pure metals. Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon.

Alloys are made by mixing metals with other elements to improve their properties. Steel is iron with carbon added — it is stronger and harder than pure iron. Bronze is copper and tin — harder than either pure metal. Brass is copper and zinc. Alloys have different sized atoms that distort the regular lattice, preventing layers from sliding easily. This makes alloys less malleable than pure metals but much stronger.

Polymers.intro: Polymers are large molecules made of many repeating units (monomers) joined together. They have distinctive properties.
Polymers.mnemonic: Remember: 'Poly means Many Monomers' — a POLYmer is made of MANY MONOmers. For the two types: 'ThermosOFTening is SOFTware (can be rewritten/re-moulded); ThermoSETting is SET in concrete (can never be changed)'.

sections.title: Polymer Structure
sections.text: Polymers are long chain molecules formed by joining many small monomer units together. Their properties depend on their chain structure and how chains interact.
points: Monomer — small repeating unit; e.g. ethene (CH₂=CH₂) is the monomer for poly(ethene)
Polymer — long chain of monomers joined by covalent bonds; e.g. poly(ethene), nylon, PVC, DNA, proteins
Addition polymerisation — alkene monomers join; double bond opens up; only one product (100% atom economy)
Condensation polymerisation — monomers join with loss of small molecule (usually water); e.g. nylon, polyester
Thermosoftening — polymer chains with weak intermolecular forces between them; melt when heated; can be remoulded
Thermosetting — chains with cross-links (strong covalent bonds between chains); do not melt; stay rigid when heated

sections.title: Properties and Uses
sections.text: The properties of polymers make them extremely versatile materials used in packaging, clothing, electronics, and medicine.
points: Thermosoftening uses — plastic bags, bottles, food packaging; can be recycled by melting and remoulding
Thermosetting uses — electrical fittings, pan handles, circuit boards; resist high temperatures
Nylon — condensation polymer; strong and tough; used in ropes, clothing, toothbrush bristles
Polyester — condensation polymer; lightweight; used in clothing, bottles (PET), resins
Environmental concern — many polymers are not biodegradable; persist in the environment for hundreds of years
Bioplastics — newer biodegradable polymers; more sustainable but often less durable

sections.title: Comparing Thermosoftening and Thermosetting
sections.text: The key difference between thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers is whether cross-links exist between the polymer chains.
points: Thermosoftening — no cross-links — chains held by weak intermolecular forces; heat breaks these; chains slide → melts
Thermosetting — cross-links present — strong covalent bonds between chains; heat cannot break them; does not melt
Structure determines use — thermosoftening can be recycled; thermosetting cannot be re-moulded
Increasing chain length — longer chains = stronger intermolecular forces = higher melting point
Branching — branched chains pack less efficiently; weaker forces; lower melting point than unbranched

keyTerms.def: A large molecule made of many repeating monomer units joined by covalent bonds
A small molecule that joins with many others to form a polymer chain
A polymer with no cross-links between chains; softens and melts when heated; can be reshaped
A polymer with covalent cross-links between chains; does not melt; remains rigid when heated
A covalent bond between polymer chains in a thermosetting polymer, preventing melting
Polymerisation where alkene monomers join together; no atoms lost; 100% atom economy
Polymerisation where monomers join with the loss of a small molecule (usually water)

examTips: Thermosoftening = NO cross-links = melts when heated = can be recycled. Thermosetting = cross-links = does NOT melt = cannot be recycled.
Thermosetting plastics are used for electrical fittings and pan handles specifically because they resist high temperatures — mention this application.
For addition polymerisation: 100% atom economy because no by-products. For condensation: less than 100% because water (or other molecule) is lost.
commonMistakes: Confusing thermosoftening and thermosetting — remember: cross-links = thermosetting = rigid and cannot be melted.
Saying addition polymers have double bonds — the monomers have double bonds, but the polymer does NOT (they are used up during polymerisation).
Forgetting that condensation polymers produce a small molecule (water) as a by-product.
clozePassages: Polymers are large molecules made of many small repeating units called monomers. They are formed by a process called polymerisation. Addition polymers are formed from alkene monomers — the double bond opens up and monomers join together in a long chain. Poly(ethene), poly(propene), and PVC are common addition polymers. Their properties depend on the monomer used and the conditions of polymerisation.

Condensation polymers are formed when monomers join together with the elimination of a small molecule — usually water. Nylon is made from diamines and dicarboxylic acids. Polyester is made from diols and dicarboxylic acids. DNA and proteins are natural condensation polymers. Unlike addition polymers, condensation polymers contain functional groups in their chain and can be broken down by hydrolysis.

Plastics are polymer materials that have many uses due to their versatile properties. Thermosoftening polymers melt when heated because the polymer chains are held together by weak intermolecular forces that break easily. Thermosetting polymers have cross-links between chains and do not melt when heated. Plastic pollution is a major environmental problem — many plastics are not biodegradable and persist in the environment for hundreds of years.

States of Matter.intro: The three states of matter — solid, liquid and gas — have different particle arrangements and properties. Changes of state involve energy changes.
States of Matter.mnemonic: Remember particle arrangements with 'Soldiers, Loungers, Ghosts': Solids = Soldiers (rigid, orderly, fixed); Liquids = Loungers (close but can move around); Gases = Ghosts (spread out, move freely, random). For energy: Heating = particles gain energy and spread out.

sections.title: Particle Model
sections.text: The particle model describes the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids, and gases.
points: Solid — particles close together in regular arrangement; vibrate in fixed positions; cannot flow; definite shape and volume
Liquid — particles close together but in random arrangement; move freely past each other; flow; definite volume, no fixed shape
Gas — particles far apart; move rapidly in all random directions; fill any container; no fixed shape or volume
Particle speed — gases move fastest; solids vibrate slowest
Intermolecular forces — strong in solids (holding fixed positions); weaker in liquids; negligible in gases

sections.title: Changes of State
sections.text: Changes of state occur when particles gain or lose enough energy to overcome the intermolecular forces. These are physical changes — no new substances are formed.
points: Melting — solid → liquid (energy absorbed; breaks forces holding particles in fixed positions)
Boiling/evaporation — liquid → gas (energy absorbed; particles gain enough energy to escape)
Condensing — gas → liquid (energy released; particles slow down and intermolecular forces re-form)
Freezing — liquid → solid (energy released; particles slow to vibrating in fixed positions)
Sublimation — solid → gas directly (e.g. dry ice/CO₂, iodine)
Physical change — changes of state are reversible; no new substance formed; same chemical formula throughout

sections.title: Energy and Changes of State
sections.text: During a change of state, the temperature stays constant even though energy is being added. The energy breaks the intermolecular forces rather than raising temperature.
points: Constant temperature during change of state — energy supplied goes into breaking intermolecular forces, not raising temperature
Heating curve — temperature rises, then flat section (melting), rises again, then flat section (boiling)
Latent heat — energy needed to change state without changing temperature
Higher melting/boiling point = stronger intermolecular forces (or stronger bonds to break)
Stronger forces = higher state-change temperatures — e.g. ionic compounds (strong forces) have very high MPs; simple molecular (weak forces) have low MPs

keyTerms.def: Temperature at which a substance changes from solid to liquid
Temperature at which a substance changes from liquid to gas throughout the bulk
A reversible change of state — no new substance formed
Direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state
Energy absorbed or released during a change of state at constant temperature
Forces of attraction between molecules — overcome when a substance melts or boils

examTips: Changes of state are PHYSICAL, not chemical changes — no new substance is formed and the change is reversible.
At melting point and boiling point, temperature stays CONSTANT — the energy is used to break intermolecular forces, not to increase temperature.
Always describe particle movement and arrangement for each state in descriptive questions — examiners expect 'vibrate in fixed positions' not just 'close together'.
commonMistakes: Saying changes of state are chemical changes — they are PHYSICAL and reversible.
Saying temperature continues to rise during melting/boiling — it stays constant while the state change occurs.
Confusing intermolecular forces (between molecules) with intramolecular bonds (within molecules) — only intermolecular forces are broken during a change of state for simple molecular substances.
clozePassages: Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid, and gas. In a solid, particles are closely packed in fixed positions and vibrate about those positions. In a liquid, particles are close together but can flow past each other. In a gas, particles are far apart and move rapidly in random directions. The state of a substance at a given temperature depends on the strength of the forces between particles.

Changes of state occur when substances are heated or cooled. Melting is the change from solid to liquid. Boiling is the change from liquid to gas. Condensation is gas to liquid. Freezing is liquid to solid. Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas. These are physical changes — no new substances are formed. The temperature at which a substance melts or boils depends on the strength of its intermolecular forces.

The melting point and boiling point of a substance reflect the strength of forces between its particles. Ionic compounds and giant covalent structures have very high melting points due to strong forces throughout the structure. Simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points because only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome. The stronger the forces between particles, the more energy is needed to change state.

Giant Covalent Structures.intro: Giant covalent structures contain millions of atoms all bonded by strong covalent bonds in a 3D lattice. This gives them extreme hardness and very high melting points.
Giant Covalent Structures.mnemonic: Remember key giant covalent structures with 'Diamonds Glow Silently' — Diamond, Graphite, Silicon dioxide. For conducting: only Graphite and Graphene conduct (they have delocalised electrons); Diamond and SiO₂ do NOT.

sections.title: Diamond
sections.text: Diamond is a giant covalent structure of carbon where each atom forms four covalent bonds. This makes it the hardest natural substance.
points: Structure — each carbon atom covalently bonded to 4 others in a tetrahedral arrangement
Hardness — very hard because every atom is held by 4 strong covalent bonds; used in cutting tools and drill bits
Very high melting point — enormous numbers of strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it
Does not conduct electricity — all 4 outer electrons are used in bonding; no free/delocalised electrons
Transparent — used as gemstones in jewellery
Insoluble in water — no charged particles to interact with water molecules

sections.title: Graphite and Graphene
sections.text: Graphite is a giant covalent structure where carbon atoms form flat hexagonal layers. Unlike diamond, it conducts electricity and is soft.
points: Graphite structure — each C bonded to 3 others in flat layers of hexagons; layers stacked on top of each other
Delocalised electrons — 1 delocalised electron per carbon atom; these move freely between layers
Conducts electricity — delocalised electrons carry charge; used as electrodes in electrolysis
Soft and slippery — layers held by weak intermolecular forces; layers slide easily; used as lubricant and in pencils
Graphene — a single layer of graphite; one atom thick; extremely strong (stronger than steel by weight)
Graphene applications — flexible electronics, composites, filters; conducts electricity and heat excellently

sections.title: Silicon Dioxide
sections.text: Silicon dioxide (SiO₂) is a giant covalent structure found in sand and quartz. Each silicon atom bonds to 4 oxygen atoms.
points: Structure — each Si bonded to 4 O atoms; each O bonded to 2 Si atoms; 3D network like diamond
Very high melting point — many strong covalent bonds throughout structure
Very hard — used as an abrasive; found in sand, quartz, glass
Does not conduct electricity — no free electrons or ions
Insoluble in water — strong covalent bonds not broken by water
Formula SiO₂ — ratio 1 Si : 2 O, reflecting the bonding arrangement

keyTerms.def: A structure where millions of atoms are all connected by strong covalent bonds in a 3D network
A giant covalent allotrope of carbon where each C atom forms 4 covalent bonds; hardest natural substance
A giant covalent allotrope of carbon with layered hexagonal structure; conducts electricity due to delocalised electrons
A single layer of graphite; one atom thick; extremely strong and highly conductive
SiO₂ — a giant covalent structure forming sand and quartz; very hard with high melting point
Different structural forms of the same element — diamond, graphite, and graphene are all allotropes of carbon

examTips: Diamond does NOT conduct; graphite DOES — the reason is delocalised electrons in graphite (diamond uses all 4 outer electrons in bonding).
Explain high melting points of giant covalent structures by saying: 'many strong covalent bonds must be broken throughout the structure — this requires a lot of energy'.
For graphite as a lubricant: say 'layers can slide over each other because they are held together by weak intermolecular forces'.
commonMistakes: Saying diamond conducts electricity — it does NOT because all 4 outer electrons are in covalent bonds with no free electrons.
Confusing why graphite has a low melting point with why it conducts — they are different explanations: low melting = weak forces between layers; conduction = delocalised electrons.
Saying SiO₂ has the same structure as NaCl — SiO₂ is giant covalent (not ionic); it does NOT conduct electricity.
clozePassages: Giant covalent structures contain millions of atoms all bonded together by strong covalent bonds. Diamond is an allotrope of carbon in which each carbon atom is bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement. This makes diamond the hardest natural substance. It has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity, as all outer electrons are used in bonding and there are no free electrons.

Graphite is another allotrope of carbon. Each carbon atom is bonded to three others in flat hexagonal layers. One electron per carbon is delocalised and can move between the layers, allowing graphite to conduct electricity. The layers are held together by weak intermolecular forces and can slide over each other, making graphite soft and useful as a lubricant. Graphene is a single layer of graphite — one atom thick — with exceptional strength and conductivity.

Silicon dioxide (SiO₂) is a giant covalent structure found in sand and quartz. Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom to two silicon atoms, forming a rigid three-dimensional network. It has a very high melting point and is very hard. Like diamond, it does not conduct electricity. The strong covalent bonds throughout the structure mean a huge amount of energy is needed to break it down.

Nanoparticles.intro: Nanoparticles are extremely small particles, 1-100 nanometres in size. Their tiny size gives them unique properties compared to the same material in bulk.
Nanoparticles.mnemonic: Think 'Nano = Tiny = Huge Surface Area' — smaller the particle, bigger the surface area to volume ratio. Remember: 1 nanometre = 1 × 10⁻⁹ metres. 'Small but MIGHTY' — nanoparticles are tiny but have enhanced properties.

sections.title: Properties of Nanoparticles
sections.text: Nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio, giving them different properties from the same material in bulk form.
points: Size: 1–100 nm — similar scale to large molecules; much smaller than bulk material
Very high surface area to volume ratio — more atoms on the surface → more reactive than bulk material
Different properties to bulk — different colour (gold nanoparticles appear red/purple, not gold), lower melting point, greater strength
Better catalysts — more surface atoms available to participate in reactions
1 nanometre = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m — about 10 atoms across

sections.title: Uses and Risks
sections.text: Nanoparticles have many current applications but also raise important questions about safety and long-term health effects.
points: Sunscreen — TiO₂ nanoparticles absorb UV; transparent unlike bulk TiO₂ (which is white)
Medical uses — drug delivery targeting cancer cells; antibacterial silver nanoparticles in wound dressings
Electronics — used in computer chips, displays, and batteries
Catalysts — platinum nanoparticles in catalytic converters; very high surface area improves efficiency
Risks — very small particles can pass through cell membranes and enter the bloodstream; long-term effects unknown
Ethical issue — benefits of nanotech vs unknown risks — more research needed before widespread use

sections.title: Uses and Concerns
sections.text: Nanoparticles are used widely in medicine, cosmetics and materials science, but their small size raises health and environmental questions.
points: Medicine — drug delivery systems; nanoparticles carry drugs directly to cancer cells
Cosmetics — titanium dioxide and zinc oxide nanoparticles in sunscreen absorb UV
Antibacterial — silver nanoparticles used in wound dressings and clothing
Electronics — carbon nanotubes used in transistors and conductive materials
Concerns — unknown long-term effects; small enough to pass through cell membranes; regulations still developing

keyTerms.def: A particle 1–100 nm in size with a very high surface area to volume ratio and unique properties
The ratio of surface area to volume — much higher in nanoparticles than in bulk material
A unit of length equal to 1 × 10⁻⁹ m; used to describe the size of nanoparticles

examTips: Nanoparticles have a high surface area to volume ratio — this is WHY they are more reactive than bulk material.
When evaluating nanoparticle use, give a balanced answer: state benefits (e.g. better drug delivery, UV protection) AND risks (unknown long-term health effects, environmental impact).
State that nanoparticles have DIFFERENT properties to the bulk material — not just 'better'.
commonMistakes: Saying nanoparticles are the same as the bulk material — their properties (colour, reactivity, melting point) are DIFFERENT at the nanoscale.
Forgetting to mention the surface area to volume ratio when explaining why nanoparticles are more reactive.
Not giving a balanced evaluation — always include both benefits AND risks of nanoparticles in 'evaluate' questions.
clozePassages: Nanoparticles are particles between 1 and 100 nanometres in size. They have a very large surface area to volume ratio compared to bulk materials, which gives them different and often enhanced properties. For example, gold normally appears yellow but gold nanoparticles appear red or purple. This change in properties at the nanoscale opens up many potential applications in medicine, electronics, and materials science.

Nanoparticles have many current and potential applications. Silver nanoparticles have antibacterial properties and are used in wound dressings and clothing. Titanium dioxide nanoparticles are used in sunscreens. Carbon nanotubes have exceptional strength and electrical conductivity. Drug delivery using nanoparticles allows medicines to be targeted directly at cancer cells, reducing side effects. Nanoparticles in catalysts increase reaction rates due to their high surface area.

Despite their potential benefits, nanoparticles raise concerns about safety. Because they are so small, they can enter the body through the skin, lungs, and digestive system. The effects of nanoparticles on human health and the environment are not fully understood. Research is ongoing to determine the risks. This highlights the need for careful regulation of new technologies and the importance of assessing both benefits and risks before widespread use.
